title: Envoys from Babylon and a Word of Exile
summary: The king of Babylon sends letters and a gift to Hezekiah after his recovery, and Hezekiah shows the envoys everything in his treasure house and armory. Isaiah announces that all of it, and some of Hezekiah's own descendants, will one day be carried off to Babylon. Hezekiah calls the word good, thinking that at least his own lifetime will be peaceful.
story: This short chapter closes the first half of Isaiah and opens the door to the second. Chapters 36 and 37 showed Hezekiah trusting God against Assyria, and chapter 38 showed God answering his prayer for life. Now the same king, flattered by attention from a distant court, puts his wealth on display. For the first time in the book, Babylon is named as the power that will carry Judah away. The next chapter begins with “Comfort, comfort My people,” addressed to a people who have experienced exactly what Isaiah predicts here. Chapter 39 is the hinge between the Assyrian crisis of Isaiah's own lifetime and the Babylonian exile that dominates the chapters that follow.
historical:
Merodach-baladan (Marduk-apla-iddina II in Babylonian records) was a Chaldean leader from southern Mesopotamia who seized the throne of Babylon and held it for about twelve years, from about 721 to 710 BC, before the Assyrian king Sargon II drove him out. He regained the city briefly around 703 BC, only to be expelled again by Sennacherib. He spent much of his career organizing resistance to Assyria, and many historians think his embassy to Hezekiah was more than a get-well visit: it was a search for allies in the west. That would place the visit before Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC, and it would explain why Hezekiah showed the envoys his armory as well as his gold. The parallel accounts are in 2 Kings 20:12-19, and 2 Chronicles 32:31 adds that God left Hezekiah to himself in this matter to test what was in his heart.

In Hezekiah's day Babylon was a restless province under Assyria, not the power that threatened Judah. The prophecy looks past that situation to a time more than a century later, when the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 597 BC, carried off the treasures of the temple and the palace along with King Jehoiachin and his court (2 Kings 24:10-16), and finally destroyed the city in 587 or 586 BC.
cultural:
Royal envoys in the ancient Near East carried letters and gifts, and exchanges of gifts between courts were a normal part of diplomacy, often signaling an alliance or a request for one. Showing a visiting delegation your treasury and your weapons was a display of strength, a way of proving you were a partner worth having. The items listed, silver, gold, spices, and precious oil, were the reserves of a kingdom, and the armory was its security. Isaiah's questions (where did they come from, what did they say, what did they see) expose the political meaning of the visit.

The word translated “eunuchs” in verse 7 could mean castrated men who served in royal households, but it was also used more broadly for court officials; the same term is applied to Potiphar in Genesis, who was married. Either way, Hezekiah's descendants would serve a foreign king rather than rule their own people. Daniel 1:3 describes young men of Judah's royal family and nobility taken to serve in the court of Nebuchadnezzar.
literary: The chapter is a compact prophetic narrative built around questions. Isaiah asks, Hezekiah answers, and each answer condemns him further: the men came from far away, from Babylon; they saw everything; there is nothing he did not show them. The word “everything” echoes through the chapter, first as the extent of Hezekiah's display (verse 2) and then as the extent of the coming loss (verse 6). The ending is deliberately unsettling. Hezekiah's reply is recorded along with his inner thought, and the narrator does not say how to judge it, leaving the reader to weigh a king who is both relieved and resigned.

outline.t: Babylonian envoys arrive and Hezekiah shows them everything
The word of the LORD: all will be carried to Babylon

doctrines.note: Hezekiah's fault is not named as a single act, but the chapter's shape shows it: pride in his possessions and a readiness to seek security in alliances rather than in the God who had just delivered him. The man who spread Sennacherib's letter before the LORD now spreads his treasures before Babylon.

The judgment announced here falls generations later. Scripture often shows the consequences of a people's choices unfolding across time, and Isaiah's word frames the exile as God's judgment rather than a mere accident of history.

Babylon, a minor player in this scene, is named as the future instrument of judgment long before it becomes an empire. The chapter prepares the reader for the second half of the book, where God will also name the instrument of Judah's release.

words.note: Otsar, treasure or storehouse. It appears in verse 2 (“his storehouses”) and again in Hezekiah's own reply in verse 4 (“my treasures”), and the related verb for storing up returns in the oracle of verse 6. What Hezekiah treats as his security and his glory becomes, in the oracle, exactly what will be taken away.

Saris, eunuch or court official. The word could refer to castrated servants of a royal household but was also used of high officials in general. Its use here stresses that the royal line of David will serve in a foreign palace rather than rule in its own.

Shalom, peace, which includes safety, wholeness, and well-being. Hezekiah hopes for “peace and security” in his lifetime. The word will return with great force in the chapters that follow, where God promises a peace that does not depend on treasuries or alliances.

christ: The chapter's connection to Christ is indirect but real. It announces the exile that would seem to end the promises to David: the king's own descendants serving in a foreign palace, the treasures gone, and later the throne itself empty. The second half of Isaiah answers that loss with promises of a return and of a Servant through whom God will restore his people. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus marks the deportation to Babylon as one of the great turning points in the line of David (Matthew 1:11-12, 17), and it presents Jesus as the son of David who comes after the exile to fulfill what had seemed lost. Hezekiah, a good king who still failed, shows why Israel needed a better one.

hard.q: Was Hezekiah's response in verse 8 selfish relief or humble acceptance?
hard.a:
Readers have taken it both ways, and the text leaves room for both. On one reading, Hezekiah is complacent: told that his children will be taken into captivity, he is glad that the trouble will come after he is gone. The narrator's report of his inner thought seems to invite that judgment, and it fits the portrait of a king whose pride was exposed in this chapter. On another reading, Hezekiah accepts God's word as just and recognizes the postponement as mercy, much as God delayed disaster in the case of Ahab's repentance (1 Kings 21:29) and Josiah's (2 Kings 22:18-20). He calls the word good because it comes from God, and he is grateful that judgment is deferred.

The chapter may be deliberately ambiguous. What is not ambiguous is the direction of the story: a faithful king has not been able to secure his people's future, and the book now turns to what God himself will do.

questions: Hezekiah trusted God in a crisis but was vulnerable to flattery in success. Why is prosperity sometimes more dangerous to faith than danger?
Isaiah's three questions exposed what Hezekiah had done. What questions might God ask about where you are looking for security?
Hezekiah was content that trouble would come after his lifetime. How do our choices today affect those who come after us?
